transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Anya Patel (CTO, VectorNorth), Rashid Khan (Senior ML Eng), Priya Menon (Infra lead)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on p95 latency targets, multi-region edge routing concerns, hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, plan for token/sec streaming benchmarks, security questions on VPC/KMS/SAML.
Topics: p95 goals, concurrency patterns, streaming vs batch token/sec, KV cache impact, fallback routing, security/SO C2 (sic), pilot plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Morgan from Redwood, AE on this. Diego who handles the deep perf stuff is with me.
[00:08] Anya: Thanks, Morgan. We've been looking at Redwood for the last couple weeks, a lot of the perf numbers look promising. Wanted to run through our p95 targets and see where Hosted vs Dedicated or Private fits.
[00:18] Morgan: Totally. Rough plan for today — your p95 targets, burst patterns, whether streaming is critical, and what security constraints you have. Then Diego will sketch benchmarking approach.
[00:27] Diego: Hi, all. Quick note, I may drop into really nitty details, feel free to stop me.
[00:32] Rashid: Cool. To set context, our product is an edge inference layer — user chatflows get routed to regional endpoints. Typical session is 120–300 tokens; but we see bursts of 2–3k tokens per second across regions during peak events. We need p95 <= 450ms for streaming 1-token increments for chat UX.
[00:48] Priya: And from infra, we want to keep egress within our VPC, avoid long hops. Private deployment preference if we can't meet p95 on hosted.
[00:59] Morgan: Good. When you say streaming 1-token p95 450ms, is that end-to-end including network and client, or server-only?
[01:05] Anya: End-to-end from our front-end to the token streamed back to user.
[01:09] Morgan: Okay that raises routing concerns — regional edge pops help. We support region-based routing and can route to closest Redwood host. For Dedicated you can reserve GPU pools within a region to minimize cross-region hops.
[01:22] Diego: On the engine side, continuous batching and KV cache matter. If your workloads reuse context heavily, prefix caching can shave 30–60% off per-token latencies. For streaming small tokens, micro-batching hurts more than helps; so we'd configure very small batch windows.
[01:38] Rashid: How deterministic is that 30–60%? Our past experience varies, sometimes it's negligible.
[01:42] Diego: It's workload dependent. With reuse of KV cache and short attention horizon, we typically see consistent gains. But for high-concurrency single-token streams, the benefit is more from optimized attention kernels and small-batch routing. Also quantized kernels help if model accuracy isn't impacted.
[01:58] Priya: Speaking of quantization, we have regulations that disallow any change in output distribution for some prompts — so lossy quantization is risky. Would Redwood enforce model variants?
[02:07] Morgan: Yes, you can pin model versions and fallbacks. We recommend dedicated capacity for constraints like that — you get predictable throughput and rollback if quality deviates.
[02:16] Anya: Can we get guaranteed p95 on Hosted? We prefer hosted for speed to production but worried about noisy neighbors during peak civic events.
[02:25] Diego: Hosted has strong SLOs, but if you need strict deterministic p95 during spikes, Dedicated or Private gives guarantees via reserved GPU pools and autoscaling policies. That said, we have routing fallback policies that can divert to replica pools to maintain availability, but latency may change.
[02:39] Morgan: Another lever is caching front-end responses for repeated prompts — reduces calls. But for live chat you can't cache much.
[02:46] Rashid: Could you walk through a benchmark you'd run to validate the 450ms p95 for 1-token streaming?
[02:51] Diego: Sure. Plan outline: 1) Replay real traffic traces you provide (or synthetic that matches token distribution), 2) run streaming token/sec harness where clients open connections and request token-by-token, measure p95 end-to-end, 3) vary concurrency from 50 to 2000 concurrent streams, and 4) test fallback routing and burst scenarios. We'll instrument TTF (time-to-first-token) and inter-token intervals.
[03:18] Morgan: We'll also need to measure cold cache vs warm KV cache and cold KV eviction rates.
[03:24] Anya: About region routing — can we pin traffic to our VPC? We have a VPC-only policy, and prefer private deployment for regulated customers.
[03:31] Priya: Yes that's key. SOC 2 is fine, but VPC endpoints + KMS for token encryption is non-negotiable.
[03:38] Morgan: Private deployments (VPC or on-prem) integrate with your KMS/HSM. We support BYO-KMS. For Hosted we provide customer keys in an HSM-backed KMS, but the network path exits our infra unless you use Private.
[03:50] Anya: Any runtime differences between Private and Dedicated?
[03:54] Diego: Runtime is identical — same inference engine, same kernel selection. Differences are around control plane and networking. Private gives you full network control and local egress. Dedicated is still in our cloud but isolated GPU pools. Performance-wise, Dedicated can be tuned for lower jitter because you reserve capacity.
[04:10] Rashid: How do autoscaling policies interact with p95 SLOs? If you scale up slowly during a burst you blow past p95.
[04:15] Diego: We expose autoscale thresholds and predictive warm-up. For Known events we can pre-warm capacity. Also policies can prioritize p95 over throughput, meaning we reject low-priority requests to keep latency SLOs.
[04:30] Priya: That rejection behavior — will it manifest as 429s? We need predictable failure modes.
[04:34] Morgan: Yes, by default 429s for rate-limited behavior. You can map fallbacks to a cheaper model rather than fail outright.
[04:41] Anya: We're also evaluating edge routing — we run a multi-region front with latency-based DNS. Could we host Redwood endpoints inside our network edge?
[04:50] Diego: We have an edge routing product for low-latency applications — it's essentially colocated endpoints that reduce hop count. For regulated data you can run Private agents in your VPC in each region.
[04:59] Rashid: For the benchmark, we need to measure tokens/sec sustained over 10 minutes at peak and p95 sampled every minute.
[05:05] Diego: Sounds good. We typically do 5 and 10 minute sustained runs and a 60-minute soak. For token/sec we instrument both tokens/sec per GPU and per endpoint, and overall latency distribution.
[05:17] Rashid: What about streaming overhead — websockets vs chunked HTTP? We prefer websockets but our infra uses HTTP/2 streams.
[05:24] Diego: We support both. Websocket has slightly lower overhead for token streaming, but HTTP/2 chunking is also efficient. We'll test both in the harness.
[05:31] Priya: Security again — do you support SAML SSO for admin console and RBAC?
[05:35] Morgan: Yes SSO via SAML and OIDC, RBAC with role scopes, audit logs. For Private you get full audit retention options.
[05:43] Anya: Any known limitations on sequence length and memory consumption that can skew p95?
[05:48] Diego: Very long sequences can push KV cache and memory usage up; some kernels scale superlinearly with seq len. We'll profile memory vs sequence and may recommend trimming context or windowed attention for long histories.
[05:59] Rashid: Do you provide token-level cost breakdowns during tests? We need to calculate unit economics — cost per 1k tokens at p95 SLA.
[06:05] Morgan: Yes our console gives token-level cost and latency breakdown, and Diego can export a per-route cost model.
[06:11] Diego: We'll also provide suggestions — batching window, quantization profile, model variants — to hit cost/latency targets.
[06:19] Anya: Who are typical competitors you see with customers like us?
[06:22] Morgan: Commonly Anthropic and OpenAI for hosted APIs; some customers still bring self-hosted stacks or Run:ai for orchestration. We try to show cost and routing wins with our unified runtime.
[06:33] Priya: Ok next steps from our side — we'll send actual traffic traces and a list of critical prompts.
[06:38] Morgan: Perfect. Diego, anything else on the benchmark plan?
[06:41] Diego: I'll include canonical scripts: streaming token harness, cold/warm KV scenarios, concurrency sweep, fallbacks to cheaper variants, and region routing stress. Expect that by Monday.
[06:51] Anya: Final question — can you do a short pilot with Dedicated for a week? We'd like to validate p95 during our weekly peak window.
[06:57] Morgan: Yes, we can propose a week-long Dedicated pilot. We'll include targets and a rollback if quality issues arise.
[07:04] Rashid: Great. Anything else?
[07:06] Morgan: I'll recap: Morgan send pricing and pilot terms; Diego send benchmark plan and harness; Rashid share traces and prompts; schedule pilot kickoff — is next Thursday okay?
[07:18] Anya: Next Thursday works. Thanks everyone.
[07:21] Morgan: Thanks.

Notes / rough timestamps for action items embedded in call. There are some minor transcription errors in acronyms (S O C 2 typed SO C2 or SAMEL). Refer to attached links: perf_spreadsheet.xlsx (placeholder), security_brief.pdf (link).

End of transcript.
